title: The busker who plays one song
allegory: Mode collapse is like a busker paid only by the tip jar: once one song reliably earns the most, the best plan is to play it all night, because the jar pays for the best song and never for variety.
map: the busker's repertoire, and how often each song gets played
the policy π: a probability for every possible completion
the reward: one score for the whole finished sequence
playing the top-tipping song all night
mode collapse: nearly all probability piled onto one high-reward completion
the manager's leash: don't play what the old you never would
the KL penalty, kl_coef · D_KL(π || π_ref), against a frozen copy of the base model
a coin for surprising the crowd, too small to matter
the entropy bonus, ent_coef = 0.001 in ARENA's RLHF

chapters.name: A beautiful curve
chapters.note: reward: up and up ... every sample: . . . . . . .

cap.1: You reward a small language model for writing full stops. The score climbs beautifully. Then you read what it writes: every sample is just dots.
cap.2: ARENA's first RLHF reward counts full stops. Within a few hundred steps mean reward climbs smoothly while every completion in the logging table converges on one string of periods.
cap.3: Reward is one scalar per finished sequence, so the objective has a global maximum and RL is good at finding it. Nothing in it asks the policy to stay a language model.

cap.1: A busker is paid only by the tip jar. One song earns the most, so they play it more, and more. By midnight it is the only song they know.
cap.2: The jar is the reward; the repertoire is the policy. A song that tips well gets its probability raised, so it gets played more, so it gets raised again.
cap.3: For a softmax policy the exact gradient on output i's logit is π_i(R_i - E[R]): mass already on a high scorer attracts more push. Rich get richer until one mode holds everything.

parts.note: how often each song is played
never more than the best song

cap.1: Your average tips blend all your songs. A blend never beats its best ingredient, and only matches it when it is pure best song. So the jar pays for collapse.
cap.2: Expected reward is a weighted average, and a weighted average is highest when all the weight sits on the top item. Reward alone is maximised by a policy that says one thing.
cap.3: max over π of E_π[R] is reached by putting all mass on argmax R. A spread-out policy is optimal only if the objective also values spread: an entropy bonus, or a KL to a reference.

curves.label: top scorer the base model writes often
top scorer the base model almost never writes

cap.1: Same leash, two tempting outputs. Nonsense the old you never played gets reined in quickly. A favourite the old you already loved sails straight through.
cap.2: Share of plays the top scorer gets as the leash tightens, left to right (illustrative). Unfamiliar text has dropped to about 3% by 0.3; familiar text still takes most plays.
cap.3: The optimum of E[R] - β·KL(π || π_ref) is π ∝ π_ref·exp(R/β). Here the top scorer beats the rest by 1 (illustrative); its prior mass multiplies straight into its share.

chapters.name: The rush transcript
chapters.note: the old you played this one too

cap.1: The manager's leash only says: don't play what the old you never would. So the busker plays the old crowd favourite all night, and the leash barely tugs.
cap.2: ARENA reports a run that collapsed onto 'This is a rush transcript…' plus a stock news opener: text common in training data, rated likely by the reference, and it scored well.
cap.3: Collapsing onto y costs about -log π_ref(y) in KL, which is small for memorised boilerplate. The penalty guards against off-distribution text, not against repetition.

chapters.name: Collapse or hacking?

left.title: Reward hacking
lines: the score is the wrong target
the model finds the scorer's mistakes

chapters.verdict: The full-stop counter does both: check kl_coef is back on, then fix the reward.

cap.1: Two different failures. Hacking: the jar rewards the wrong thing. Collapse: even a fair jar ends with one song. A full-stop counter manages both.
cap.2: First check kl_coef is back on (2.5; the plumbing test sets 0.0). Then fix the reward: count tokens containing a period, or normalise by length. Log samples every phase.
cap.3: ent_coef = 0.001 in ARENA's RLHF is far too weak to spread mass back out once it concentrates. Reward and coherence come apart quietly: log samples next to the curve.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: An average is maximised by one answer
The leash stops gibberish, not repetition
Read the samples, not just the curve

cap.1: Tune a model with rewards and it will happily become a one-song busker. Spotting that, and paying for variety, is part of steering AI.
cap.2: Any fine-tune against one score pulls outputs towards a few high-scoring phrasings. Variety has to be protected in the objective, and checked by reading outputs.
cap.3: For steering and evals: falling output entropy, or repeated samples while reward rises, means the optimiser found a narrow mode. Judge a run by samples and KL, not reward alone.

coda.title: Share out the busker's plays: set the leash, and how familiar the stock opener is

params.label: how often the base model writes the stock opener

readouts.label: ordinary varied text keeps
readouts.f: (100*softmax([log(0.0001) + 1/leash, log(fam) + 0.7/leash, log(0.05) + 0.5/leash, log(0.9499 - fam) + 0.3/leash])[3]).toFixed(0) + '% of plays'

readouts.label: leash cost, KL in nats
readouts.f: (p => sum(p.map((v, i) => v > 0 ? v*log(v/[0.0001, fam, 0.05, 0.9499 - fam][i]) : 0)))(softmax([log(0.0001) + 1/leash, log(fam) + 0.7/leash, log(0.05) + 0.5/leash, log(0.9499 - fam) + 0.3/leash])).toFixed(2)

caption.1: Drag the leash strength down and watch dots only take every play. Then set it around 0.3 and raise how familiar the stock opener is: it takes the lead anyway.
caption.2: Each bar is a share of plays at the best policy for this leash (toy scores 1, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3). Loose leash: the top scorer wins. Tight leash: back to the base model, habits included.
caption.3: Bars are π ∝ π_ref·exp(R/β), the optimum of E[R] - β·KL(π || π_ref). A mode with high prior mass wins at low KL cost: watch the KL readout stay small as it takes over.

where_else: GANs, where the generator settles on one output that reliably fools the current discriminator
Policy-gradient agents that lock onto one action too early, which PPO's entropy bonus is there to prevent
Greedy or low-temperature decoding looping on one phrase: the same narrowing, done at sampling time

hamming.what: Mode collapse is an RL-tuned policy piling nearly all its probability onto one or a few high-reward outputs and producing nothing else.
hamming.when: In RLHF-style fine-tuning against a single score, especially with a weak entropy bonus, a loose KL leash, or a reward with one easy maximum.
hamming.why: An average reward is maximised by putting all probability on the best-scoring output, so collapse is the optimiser succeeding at the objective exactly as written.

object.title: The repertoire rack
object.subtitle: Eight kinds of output, eight leash settings: how the plays share out as the leash goes from tight to loose.

knobs.label: How often the base model writes the stock opener

cap.1: Each row is one leash setting, each column one kind of output. Bar height is the share of plays it gets. Tight leash at the front, loose at the back.
cap.2: Heights are the best policy's probabilities at each β, with illustrative scores: dots only 1, stock opener 0.7, short punchy 0.5, the five ordinary kinds 0.3.
cap.3: Row r plots π ∝ π_ref·exp(R/β_r), with β falling geometrically from 1 to 0.03. π_ref: dots 0.0001, stock opener 0.02, short punchy 0.05, the rest shared evenly.

cap.1: Front rows, tight leash: the plays spread across all the ordinary kinds, just like the old repertoire. Plenty of variety.
cap.2: At large β the KL term dominates and the policy stays close to the reference: the five ordinary outputs share most of the mass.
cap.3: As β grows, π tends to π_ref: the leash returns the base model, whatever habits it had.

cap.1: Middle rows: the stock opener shoots up. It scores well, and the old you already played it now and then, so the leash objects far less.
cap.2: Around β 0.08 to 0.14 the stock opener takes the largest share: its head start in π_ref lets it lead before dots only can.
cap.3: A mode wins when its log π_ref + R/β beats the rest: prior mass buys it the lead before the top scorer, whose prior is tiny, can compete.

cap.1: Back rows, leash nearly off: dots only takes almost every play. The top scorer wins outright, however strange it is.
cap.2: At small β reward dominates, and the policy piles onto argmax R regardless of how unlikely the reference finds it.
cap.3: As β tends to 0, π tends to a point mass on argmax R: the unregularised optimum, full collapse.

cap.1: Now make the stock opener more familiar to the base model. Its tall bars march to the front, and even a tight leash only pulls it back to the old habit.
cap.2: Raising π_ref for the stock opener widens the band of β where it dominates. Tight or loose, the leash cannot tell a favourite from a rut.
cap.3: Its share is set by π_ref·exp(R/β), so prior mass and reward trade off multiplicatively; memorised boilerplate is exactly the high-prior case.

predict.q: No leash and no variety bonus. What does the best policy do?

options.t: Puts all its probability on the top scorer
Spreads evenly across the good outputs

predict.why: Expected reward is an average, and an average peaks when all the weight sits on the best item.

predict.q: A phrase the base model writes often also scores well. Does the KL leash stop collapse onto it?

options.t: Barely: collapsing onto it costs little KL

predict.why: D_KL(π || π_ref) charges for text the reference finds unlikely. Text it already finds likely is cheap to repeat.

predict.q: Reward climbs smoothly for the whole run. What do you check first?

options.t: Nothing: the curve says it works

predict.why: Reward and coherence come apart quietly, and only the samples show the collapse.

object.where: Anywhere one score is optimised hard: GAN generators, greedy decoding loops, and any agent that stops exploring.
